78.title: Stephen (Acts 6:8–7:60)
78.hook: the first to die for the faith forgives his killers as the stones fall
78.carry: lay not this sin to their charge
78.howItsDone: Christians honor Stephen as the first martyr, with a feast day on December 26 in Western churches and December 27 in many Orthodox churches. His dying prayer of forgiveness is often read alongside Jesus's words from the cross.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beggar at the Beautiful Gate, walking and leaping. Your line was such as I have, give I thee. What did you give, when you had no cash? Day seventy-eight.
screen: `SUCH AS I HAVE, GIVE I THEE.`

segments.voice: Back to the argument about widows being left out of the daily food. The apostles ask the believers to choose seven people to run the tables. The first name on the list is Stephen, a man, Acts says, full of faith and of the Holy Spirit. He's a food organizer. But he's also a speaker, and he gets into fierce debates in a Jerusalem synagogue, all of them Jews, arguing about Jesus, the temple and the law. It ends with Stephen hauled before the council, where witnesses Acts calls false swear he's been speaking against the holy place. Everyone in the room turns to look at him. And Luke says they saw his face as it had been the face of an angel.
screen: `SEVEN TO RUN THE TABLES.` → `A FIERCE DEBATE.` → `THE FACE OF AN ANGEL.`

segments.voice: Stephen answers with a long speech: the history of his people, from Abraham to Moses to the temple, and in it God keeps meeting them far from any temple, in Mesopotamia, in Egypt, in the wilderness. By the end the room is furious. Stephen looks up and says he sees heaven opened, and Jesus standing at God's right hand. They cover their ears, drag him outside the city, and stone him. And while the stones fall, he prays two things. "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." And then, kneeling, loudly: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." Those may sound familiar. On the cross, in Luke's Gospel, Jesus prays, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do," and then commits his spirit into his Father's hands. Luke tells Stephen's death as an echo of his teacher's. Now today's word. Martyr comes from the Greek martys, and it first meant simply a witness, someone who tells a court what they saw. Stephen is remembered as the first Christian martyr, and over time the word slowly changed, until it meant a witness who dies rather than take back what they saw. It's worth saying clearly: this was a bitter quarrel among Jews, since Stephen and the believers around him were Jews, and not a story about one people against another. And there's a quiet detail at the edge of the scene. The witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul. Hold on to that name. Church tradition keeps his feast just after Christmas.
screen: `A HISTORY, TOLD TO THE COUNCIL.` · `LORD JESUS, RECEIVE MY SPIRIT.` · `MARTYS: A WITNESS.` · `COATS AT THE FEET OF SAUL.` · then, large: `LAY NOT THIS SIN TO THEIR CHARGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: forgive one person in your heart. Sit, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind someone who has hurt you. Not necessarily the biggest wound; one you can hold for two minutes. You don't have to tell them. You don't have to say it was fine. Stephen didn't say that. He asked that it not be held against them. See if you can let go of the charge for these two minutes, even a little. If you pray, you can use his words. If you don't, just loosen your grip. The bell holds the time.
Martyr. From the Greek martys, a witness. Stephen, remembered as the first, who forgave as he died.
Your line: lay not this sin to their charge. Today, when a grudge rises, try saying the line under your breath before anything else. Tomorrow, a chariot on a desert road. Day seventy-eight.

79.title: Philip and the Ethiopian (Acts 8:26–40)
79.hook: an African official reads Isaiah in his chariot and asks, what hinders me?
79.howItsDone: Christians often read the story of Philip and the Ethiopian as a picture of the good news reaching Africa and of baptism welcoming someone once kept at the edge. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church holds the story especially dear.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Stephen, remembered as the first martyr, a witness to the end. Your line was lay not this sin to their charge. Did you loosen your grip on one grudge? Day seventy-nine.
screen: `LAY NOT THIS SIN TO THEIR CHARGE.`

segments.voice: Ever been stuck on a page? A contract, a tax form, a poem for school, a medicine label. You read it three times and the words just sit there. Now go to a desert road running south from Jerusalem toward Gaza. A chariot is rolling along, carrying a very important man: the treasurer of the queen of the Ethiopians, a court official in charge of all her wealth. He's been to Jerusalem to worship, a long trip from Africa, and now, heading home, he's reading a scroll of the prophet Isaiah out loud. And he's stuck. Meanwhile an angel has told Philip, one of the seven food organizers, to go and stand on that road. Just that. Go and stand there.
screen: `STUCK ON A PAGE.` → `A CHARIOT ON THE DESERT ROAD.` → `GO AND STAND THERE.`

segments.voice: The Spirit tells Philip to go up to the chariot, so he runs alongside it and hears the man reading. And he asks, in the King James Bible: "Understandest thou what thou readest?" The official's answer is plain: "How can I, except some man should guide me?" He invites Philip up. The passage is Isaiah's song of the suffering servant: led like a sheep to the slaughter, silent, humiliated. Who is the prophet talking about, the man asks, himself or someone else? And Philip, starting from that page, tells him about Jesus. There's something else in the background. The official is called a eunuch, and Deuteronomy says a eunuch may not enter the assembly of the Lord. But a few chapters further on in the very scroll he's holding, God promises eunuchs who keep his covenant a place, and a name that will never be cut off. Whether he'd read that far, the text doesn't say. Then they pass some water by the road, and he asks the question of the day: "See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?" What's stopping me? In the King James text, Philip's only condition is that he believe with all his heart. Then they stop the chariot, go down into the water, and he's baptized. Philip is suddenly gone, and the official goes on his way rejoicing. Scholars think the Ethiopia of Acts was the kingdom of Kush, south of Egypt, in what's now Sudan. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church treasures the story all the same. And some readers hear in it a quiet echo of Pentecost: the good news heading out toward the ends of the earth, one reader at a time.
screen: `UNDERSTANDEST THOU WHAT THOU READEST?` · `HOW CAN I, EXCEPT SOME MAN GUIDE ME?` · `A PLACE PROMISED IN ISAIAH.` · `WHAT DOTH HINDER ME?` · then, large: `HE WENT ON HIS WAY REJOICING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: explain something kindly to someone. Sit, and breathe. Think of someone who's stuck on something you understand. A kid with homework, a parent with a phone, a new coworker, a friend with a form. Notice how Philip does it. He runs to catch up. He asks a question first. He starts from the exact page they're on, not from where he'd like to start. Picture doing that, gently, without a sigh. If you pray, you can pray for that person. The bell holds the time.
Philip and the Ethiopian. A treasurer stuck on a page of Isaiah, a stranger who runs alongside, and water by the road.
Your line: what hinders you? Today, help one person with one page, starting where they are. Tomorrow, the young man who held the coats meets a light on the road. Day seventy-nine.

80.title: The road to Damascus (Acts 9:1–9)
80.hook: Saul, hunting Christians, is blinded by light and hears: why persecute me?
80.howItsDone: Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches, among others, keep the Feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul on January 25. Many Christians speak of their own conversion as a turning, whether sudden like Paul's or slow over years.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Philip and the Ethiopian, and a question by the water. Your line was what hinders you? Whose page did you help with? Day eighty.

Remember the young man holding the coats while Stephen died? His name is Saul, and he's no bystander anymore. Acts says he's breathing out threats and slaughter against the followers of Jesus, who at this point call their movement simply the Way. He goes to the high priest and asks for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, a week's journey north, so that any followers he finds there, men or women, can be brought back to Jerusalem in chains. He's certain. He's organized. He's on the road with his papers and his companions. And just outside Damascus, in the middle of the day, a light from heaven flashes all around him, and he falls to the ground.
screen: `THE YOUNG MAN WITH THE COATS.` → `LETTERS FOR DAMASCUS.` → `A LIGHT, AND HE FALLS.`

segments.voice: Lying in the dust, he hears a voice. In the King James Bible: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" He asks, "Who art thou, Lord?" And the answer: "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest." Listen to that word me. Saul has never met Jesus. He's been hunting Jesus's followers. And the voice says, you're doing it to me. Christians have heard in that line, for two thousand years, that what's done to his people is done to him. Saul gets up, opens his eyes, and sees nothing. The men with him lead him by the hand into the city, and for three days he's blind, and doesn't eat or drink. The man who came to drag people out in chains is led in by the hand. Today's word is conversion. It comes from the Latin for turning around, and the Greek word Acts uses elsewhere means the same: a turning. Now two things people usually get wrong. There's no horse. Famous paintings put him on one, but the text only says he fell to the ground. And God doesn't rename him Paul here. Later, Acts simply says Saul, who also is called Paul: a Hebrew name and a Roman one, used side by side. Paul himself, in his letters, describes this moment less as leaving his people's faith and more as a calling, the way God called the prophets. Scholars still discuss how best to describe it. Luke thought the moment mattered so much that Acts tells it three times. And many churches keep a feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul on January twenty-fifth. The hunter becomes the one who carries the news. The road can turn.
screen: `WHY PERSECUTEST THOU ME?` · `LED BY THE HAND, BLIND.` · `CONVERSION: A TURNING AROUND.` · `NO HORSE. NO NEW NAME.` · then, large: `THE ROAD CAN TURN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop and listen for one minute. Saul only heard the voice because he was stopped. So stop. Put everything down, sit still, and close your eyes if that's comfortable. Listen to what's actually around you: traffic, a fridge, birds, your own breathing. Then listen inside: is there something you've been very sure about, charging down the road with, that might need a second look? Don't argue with it. Just listen. If you pray, you can ask, as Saul did, who are you, Lord? The bell holds the time.
Conversion. A turning around. Saul on the road to Damascus, stopped in the dust and led by the hand.
Your line: the road can turn. Today, when you're sure of something about a person, leave one inch of room for the road to turn. Tomorrow, someone has to go and knock on Saul's door. Day eighty.

81.title: Ananias (Acts 9:10–19)
81.hook: a frightened believer is sent to heal his enemy and calls him "brother Saul"
81.howItsDone: Christians in many churches call one another brother and sister, a habit that goes back to the first believers. Ananias of Damascus is honored as a saint in Catholic and Orthodox churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, conversion: Saul in the dust on the road to Damascus, led into the city blind. Your line was the road can turn. Where did you leave an inch of room? Day eighty-one.

Here's a job nobody would volunteer for: knock on the door of the one person in town you're most afraid of. Not to argue. To help. That's the job handed to a man named Ananias. He's an ordinary follower of Jesus in Damascus, not an apostle, and we know almost nothing else about him. In a vision the Lord calls his name, and he answers, here I am. Then come the instructions, specific as a delivery address: go to the street called Straight, to the house of Judas, and ask for a man from Tarsus named Saul. He's praying. And he's seen a vision of a man named Ananias coming to lay hands on him so he can see again. Ananias knows exactly who Saul is.
screen: `KNOCK ON THAT DOOR.` → `THE STREET CALLED STRAIGHT.` → `ASK FOR SAUL.`

segments.voice: So Ananias objects. In the King James Bible: "Lord, I have heard by many of this man, how much evil he hath done to thy saints at Jerusalem." And he came here with papers to arrest us. I like that he says it. The Bible keeps a lot of honest objections. And the answer comes back: go, "for he is a chosen vessel unto me." Not, he's harmless. Just, go. So he goes. Walks the street called Straight, finds the house, and walks into the room where the man the believers dread is sitting blind. Lays his hands on him. And the first words out of his mouth are these: "Brother Saul, the Lord, even Jesus, that appeared unto thee in the way as thou camest, hath sent me." Brother. Before Saul has done a single thing to earn it. Before anyone knows if he's for real. The man who came to take Ananias away in chains is greeted as family. And then, Luke says, something like scales fell from Saul's eyes, and he could see. That's where our English saying comes from: the scales fell from my eyes. He gets up, he's baptized, and he eats, for the first time in three days. The famous one in this story is Saul, who'll become Paul, whose letters are in the New Testament. But Paul's sight comes back through the hands of a man Acts names in only two places, who was scared, said so, and went anyway. And his first two words are the line for today. Brother Saul.
screen: `LORD, I HAVE HEARD OF THIS MAN.` · `A CHOSEN VESSEL. GO.` · `SCALES FALL FROM HIS EYES.` · `A NOBODY, SCARED, WHO WENT.` · then, large: `BROTHER SAUL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: call someone brother or sister. Sit, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you keep at a distance. Not someone dangerous; someone you've quietly decided isn't one of us. A neighbor, a relative, a coworker on the other side of some argument. Say their name in your head, and put brother or sister in front of it. Notice what happens in you. Resistance, maybe. Or a softening. Just notice. If you pray, you can pray for them by that name. The bell holds the time.
Ananias. The frightened disciple in Damascus who went anyway, laid his hands on his enemy, and called him brother.
Your line: brother saul. Today, give one person you've kept at a distance a word of family: a warm greeting, their name said kindly. Tomorrow, a rooftop vision and a Roman's door. Day eighty-one.

82.title: Peter and Cornelius (Acts 10)
82.hook: a rooftop vision tells Peter no one is unclean, and he walks into a Roman's house
82.howItsDone: Christians read the story of Peter and Cornelius as the moment the early church welcomed Gentiles as they were. Christian churches generally do not keep the biblical food laws, and many point to this chapter and to Acts 15 as the reason.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ananias, who was scared and went anyway. Your line was brother saul. Who got a word of family from you? Day eighty-two.

Two men, two towns on the same coast, two visions a day apart. In Caesarea, a Roman port, lives Cornelius, a centurion, an officer in the Roman army. He isn't Jewish, but he honors the God of Israel, prays, and gives generously to the poor. At three in the afternoon an angel tells him: send to Joppa for a man called Simon Peter. Down the coast in Joppa, the next day at noon, Peter climbs onto a flat roof to pray while lunch is being made. He's hungry. And he falls into a trance: a great sheet is let down from the sky, full of every kind of animal, including ones the law of Moses says a Jew must not eat. And a voice says: rise, Peter. Kill, and eat.
screen: `A ROMAN OFFICER PRAYS.` → `A HUNGRY MAN ON A ROOF.` → `RISE, PETER. KILL, AND EAT.`

segments.voice: Peter says no. Not so, Lord, I've never eaten anything common or unclean. And the voice answers, in the King James Bible: "What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common." It happens three times. Then the sheet is gone, and Peter is sitting there puzzled, and at that very moment Cornelius's messengers are standing at the gate, calling out for him. Today's word is Gentile. It comes from the Latin for nations, translating the Hebrew and Greek words for the peoples of the world: anyone who isn't Jewish. Peter himself tells Cornelius that it was not lawful for a Jew to keep company with someone of another nation, or to come into his house. He goes anyway. He walks into the Roman officer's house, full of family and friends, and he explains what the vision meant. He's worked out that it wasn't really about lunch: "God hath shewed me that I should not call any man common or unclean." Then he says, "Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons." God doesn't play favorites. While he's still speaking, the Spirit falls on everyone listening, Gentiles included, and the believers who came with Peter are astonished. Christians have read this chapter as the moment the church learned it could welcome Gentiles as they were, without asking them to become Jewish first, and many also read it as releasing Christians from the food laws. The argument wasn't over; Acts shows the church meeting in Jerusalem to settle it a few chapters later. And for Jews who keep them, then and now, those laws are part of their covenant with God. This story is about a door, and who's allowed through it.
screen: `WHAT GOD HATH CLEANSED.` · `GENTILE: THE NATIONS.` · `PETER WALKS IN.` · `NO RESPECTER OF PERSONS.` · then, large: `CALL NO ONE COMMON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: enter a door you've avoided. Sit, and breathe. Think of a door you don't go through. Maybe a real one: a neighbor's, a place of worship not your own, a part of town. Maybe a conversation you keep stepping around. Picture yourself standing outside it, hearing a knock, the way Peter did. What would it take to walk in, respectfully, as a guest? You don't have to decide today. Just stand at the door for a while. If you pray, you can bring it to God. The bell holds the time.
Gentile. From the Latin for the nations: anyone who isn't Jewish. The day Peter walked into a Roman's house.
Your line: call no one common. Today, catch the moment you file someone as not my kind of person, and take the label off. Tomorrow, a knock at another door. Day eighty-two.

83.title: Rhoda at the door (Acts 12:1–17)
83.hook: Peter escapes prison, knocks, and the maid is so happy she forgets to open
83.howItsDone: Christians often tell the story of Rhoda with a smile, as a picture of praying hard and then being surprised by the answer. Catholics and others read Peter's escape on the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, June 29.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter and Cornelius, and the old word Gentile. Your line was call no one common. Whose label did you take off? Day eighty-three.

This one starts dark. King Herod, a later Herod than the one in the Christmas story, has James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword. Seeing that it pleases some people, he arrests Peter too, during the Passover week, and plans to bring him out for a public trial when the festival's over. Peter is guarded by four squads of soldiers. The night before the trial he's asleep between two of them, chained to both. And across the city, in a house belonging to a woman named Mary, the mother of John Mark, the church is gathered, praying for him, deep into the night. In the King James Bible: "prayer was made without ceasing of the church unto God for him." Hold on to that. They're praying for exactly this.
screen: `JAMES IS KILLED.` → `PETER IN CHAINS.` → `PRAYER WITHOUT CEASING.`

segments.voice: In the prison, a light. An angel nudges Peter in the side and says, get up, quickly. The chains fall off his wrists. Put on your belt, the angel says, and your sandals. Now your cloak. Follow me. Peter follows, half asleep, sure he's dreaming. Past the first guard, past the second, to the iron gate into the city, which opens by itself. They walk one street, and the angel is gone. And Peter comes to himself in the cool night air and realizes: this is real. So he goes to Mary's house, where they're all praying, and knocks at the outer gate. A servant girl comes to answer. Her name is Rhoda, and it means rose. And here's Luke's line: "And when she knew Peter's voice, she opened not the gate for gladness, but ran in, and told how Peter stood before the gate." She's so happy she forgets to open the door. She runs in to tell everybody. And the room full of people praying for Peter's release says, in the King James: "Thou art mad." She insists. Then it must be his angel, they say. Meanwhile, outside, a wanted man stands in the street: "But Peter continued knocking." When they finally open it, they're astonished. Notice two things. First, Luke gives the servant girl a name. In a story full of kings, soldiers and apostles, the one who recognizes the voice is Rhoda, and she's remembered. Second, the church prayed hard, and when the answer came, it was standing on the doorstep, and they almost didn't let it in.
screen: `CHAINS FALL. FOLLOW ME.` · `SHE OPENED NOT THE GATE FOR GLADNESS.` · `THOU ART MAD.` · `BUT PETER CONTINUED KNOCKING.` · then, large: `ANSWERED PRAYERS KNOCK TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: laugh at one good surprise. Sit, and breathe. Think back over the last month or so for something good that arrived, that you'd hoped for, and then nearly missed, or didn't believe at first. A message you left unread. Good news you second-guessed. Someone's kindness you assumed must be a mistake. Let yourself smile at it, or laugh, the way you'd laugh at Rhoda running in with the door still shut. If you pray, you can say thank you. The bell holds the time.
Rhoda at the door. A servant girl so glad she forgot to open it, and a room that called her mad.

Your line: answered prayers knock too. Today, open the door to one good thing you've been treating as too good to be true. Tomorrow, a purple-cloth merchant, and singing at midnight. Day eighty-three.

84.title: Lydia and the jailer (Acts 16)
84.hook: a purple-cloth businesswoman opens her home; a jailer finds Paul and Silas singing at midnight
84.howItsDone: Many Christians sing hymns and psalms in hard times, and some prison ministries point to Paul and Silas singing at midnight. Lydia is honored as a saint by Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rhoda at the door, too glad to open it. Your line was answered prayers knock too. What good thing did you let in? Twelve weeks on the path. Day eighty-four.

Two people, one city, and they could hardly be more different. The city is Philippi, a Roman colony in northern Greece. Paul and his friend Silas have crossed the sea to get there after Paul dreamed of a man begging, come over and help us. On the Sabbath they go down to the river, to a place where people gather to pray, and sit and talk with the women there. One of them is a businesswoman, a dealer in purple cloth, a costly fabric. Later in the same chapter, the other person will be a prison guard, standing in the dark with a sword in his hand. Both of them end the story with the same people at their table.
screen: `COME OVER AND HELP US.` → `WOMEN BY THE RIVER.` → `A GUARD WITH A SWORD.`

segments.voice: Here's Luke on the first one, in the King James Bible: "Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened." She's a foreigner, a merchant, and a woman who runs her own household, and she's baptized with everyone in it. Then she won't take no for an answer: come into my house, and stay. Luke says she constrained them. Her home becomes the believers' meeting place in Philippi. Now the other side of town. Paul drives a spirit out of a slave girl whose fortune-telling earned her owners money, and her owners are furious. They drag Paul and Silas to the magistrates. The two are stripped, beaten with rods, and thrown into the inner prison with their feet in the stocks. Bleeding, in the dark, sore to the bone. And then: "at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them." The other prisoners are lying there listening. An earthquake shakes the prison, the doors fly open, everyone's chains come loose. The jailer wakes, sees the open doors, and draws his sword to kill himself, sure his prisoners have fled. Paul shouts: "Do thyself no harm: for we are all here." Nobody ran. The jailer falls down trembling and asks, what must I do to be saved? That night he washes their wounds, he and his household are baptized, and he sets food in front of them, rejoicing. A merchant's house and a jailer's house, both opened in one chapter. And the hinge of it all is two beaten men singing in the dark.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing something in a dark moment. Sit, and breathe. Think of a hard thing you're in right now, big or small. Let it be there. Then find a song. A hymn if you know one, or a lullaby, or anything that has ever steadied you. Hum it quietly, or sing a line under your breath. It doesn't have to be good. Paul and Silas weren't auditioning. If you pray, you can let the song be your prayer. Notice whether the dark feels any different with a tune in it. The bell holds the time.
Lydia and the jailer. Two households opened in one city. This week: Stephen the martyr, a chariot, a road, Ananias, a Gentile's door, Rhoda, and a song at midnight.
Your line: sing at midnight. Today, when something goes dark, hum one line of something good before you do anything else. Tomorrow, Paul quotes the poets of Athens. Day eighty-four.

fork.setup: you're Paul. an earthquake has opened every door and loosed every chain. the jailer is about to fall on his sword. what do you do?
options: slip out quietly while you can.
shout to him: do yourself no harm, we're all here.
wait to see what the magistrates decide.
fork.reveal: Paul cries out: do thyself no harm: for we are all here. that night the jailer washes their wounds and feeds them.

original.note: Greek: a seller of purple, Luke's one-word job title for Lydia. Purple cloth was a luxury.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a prison earthquake.
what it means: a merchant woman and a jailer both open their homes, and the hinge between them is two beaten men singing in the dark.
what a scholar hears: porphyropolis, a dealer in purple, from Thyatira; Philippi was a Roman colony, which is why its magistrates matter to the story.
